summary: Vision is a web app that lets an astronaut test their own eyesight, alone, with no operator and no internet. NASA tracks Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS): about 70% of long-mission crew show signs of it, and many report worse near vision. Yet eyesight is checked only a few times per mission. Vision fills the gap between those checks, so a crew member can test any day. The app shows Landolt C rings (the test where you say which way the ring opens). The rings are sized to the real screen, calibrated once with a bank card, and to the real distance, which the camera measures with the Google MediaPipe face model. It does not just give a score. It builds a personal baseline from the person's own first tests, then flags a result that is worse twice in a row and says what to do: carry on, repeat tomorrow, or switch to spare glasses and tell the doctor. It runs offline on any computer with a keyboard. A Raspberry Pi camera is optional. The same tool helps people far from an eye doctor on Earth.
details:
What it does and how it works. Vision is a pilot prototype for monitoring functional vision change. A test is one flow in three steps. (1) You: a participant code (never a name), which eye, glasses on or off. (2) Screen: the user holds a bank card (ISO/IEC 7810, a known size) against the screen and matches an outline, so the app knows the size of a millimetre. (3) Distance: the camera finds the eyes with the Google MediaPipe Face Landmarker and measures the distance to the screen, using the iris (11.7 mm) as a ruler. A tape check at 50 cm gives a precise camera calibration. The app tests near vision at 40 cm by default when the screen can draw that size, otherwise it suggests 1 m. During the test the camera keeps watching the distance, and the test gives no score if the face is lost or the screen cannot draw the next ring size.

The test is a staircase of Landolt C rings: a fast descent, then five signs per level until fewer than three of five are right. The user answers with arrow keys, taps or clicks. Each result is saved in the browser and can be exported as CSV.

The main idea: compare a person with themselves. Most online eye tests guess. Vision builds a personal baseline from the first five measured tests (same person, eye, glasses and distance) and uses a prediction interval, never narrower than 0.10 logMAR. A result worse than the band once means "repeat tomorrow the same way". Worse twice in a row means "persistent change: next spare glasses, note the date, tell the doctor". Better results never raise an alarm, because practice improves scores. This way a real change is spotted and a bad day is ignored.

Benefits and impact. Astronauts can check their eyes any day, alone. Mission doctors can see how vision changes over time. The tool works anywhere an eye doctor is far away: polar stations, remote villages, expeditions. It needs no install and no internet, and camera frames are processed in the browser and never stored. Participants are recorded by code only.

Tools. JavaScript in the browser (no build step, no framework), Node.js for the local server and tests, Python for the analysis script (pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib) and the optional Raspberry Pi camera server (picamera2, OpenCV), Google MediaPipe Tasks Vision 1.1.1 with the Face Landmarker model (Apache-2.0), hosted on GitHub Pages. Automated tests cover the app logic and the Pi camera server.

What we considered. Honesty about limits: it is a prototype that monitors functional vision change; it does not detect any condition and does not measure diopters. It is not yet tested in microgravity or in a clinic, no measurements on people have been made yet, and the camera distance accuracy is not yet measured (an estimate until the tape check, up to about 20% off). The app reports "Beyond screen" instead of a number when pixels are too big. Next steps: test with real people against a real eye chart, ask eye doctors to turn our rules into medical-grade ones, compare with NASA's own SANS research, and try daily checks on a long expedition on Earth.
